source: Bayardo and Schrag (1997) Using CSP look-back techniques to solve real-world SAT instances
finding: Adding backjumping and learned no-goods to plain DPLL made hard real-world SAT instances solvable. Recording derived clauses, bounded by size or by relevance, was the key.
numbers: DIMACS hanoi4: naive DPLL fails 100%; size-bounded learning order 3 fails 94%, order 4 fails 92%; relsat(3) fails 79%; relsat(4) fails 13%; best variant fails 1%. 4blocks planning: relsat(3) fails 34%, relsat(4) fails 17% at a cutoff near the mean run time.
quote: Learning schemes, through the recording of derived clauses, can create constrained search-sub-spaces
limits: Few instances, cutoff-dependent failure rates, 1997 hardware. Order-4 size-bounding was slower than order 3 on one instance because of overhead.
agent_relevance: First source for the no-good idea: keep a short reason a branch failed and reuse it. Relevance-bounded storage (drop a lesson once it no longer applies) maps to retiring stale lessons.

source: Bayardo and Schrag (1997) Using CSP look-back techniques to solve real-world SAT instances (scheduling and cutoff effect)
finding: On job-shop scheduling instances relsat(4) was 100% successful on 4 of 6 instances; the other two had failure rates that fell with a longer cutoff. Simple randomised sampling (ISAMP) beat it on these six but solved no other family.
numbers: Scheduling e0-10-by-5-1 and en-10-by-5-1: failure 21% and 18% at the base cutoff, 3% and 1% at 30 minutes. ISAMP about 10x faster than relsat(4) on the six, 100% success.
limits: A method that wins on one family can win nowhere else.
agent_relevance: Supports the portfolio rule: a store of lessons is not best everywhere; keep a cheap random-sampling arm for families with many solutions.

source: Marques-Silva and Sakallah (1999) GRASP: a search algorithm for propositional satisfiability
finding: GRASP introduced conflict analysis on the implication graph, learned conflict clauses and non-chronological (conflict-directed) backjumping. The learned clause names only the decisions that caused the conflict, so the search jumps past irrelevant decisions.
numbers: Evaluated on EDA benchmarks (test-pattern generation families SSA and BF) with a 10,000 CPU-second limit; the paper reports far fewer aborted instances and fewer backtracks than POSIT and other solvers of the time. I did not extract per-family counts.
limits: Circuit test-generation benchmarks only. No claim about language tasks.
agent_relevance: The core mechanism to copy: from a failure, find the few choices that jointly caused it, store that set as a rule, and jump back to the earliest culprit instead of the last step.

source: Katebi, Sakallah, Marques-Silva (2011) Empirical study of the anatomy of modern SAT solvers
finding: Ablation of four CDCL features in MiniSat. Clause learning mattered most, then VSIDS, then two-watched-literals, then restarts.
numbers: 1000 CNF instances from 12 application families, 10 shuffled versions each, 15 MiniSat configurations, 150,000 runs, 1000 s limit. Instances solved: no clause learning 4837; no VSIDS 6932; no 2-watched-literals 8409; no restarts 8653.
quote: disabling clause learning yields the worst performance (finishing on only 4837 instances)
limits: One solver base (MiniSat), application benchmarks only. Including a feature does not always beat excluding it.
agent_relevance: Prioritise the lesson store over restarts: restarts alone add little, a store of failures adds a lot.

source: Beame, Kautz, Sabharwal (2004) Towards understanding and harnessing the potential of clause learning
finding: Clause learning as a proof system is exponentially stronger than regular and Davis-Putnam resolution under a new learning scheme. A variant with unlimited restarts is as strong as general resolution. Using problem structure to guide learning gave exponential speed-ups on grid and pebbling formulas.
numbers: Theory plus experiments: exponential speed-ups on grid and randomized pebbling problems; substantial gains on ordering formulas.
limits: Proof-size results do not say how often a real solver finds the short proof; it needs a good branching order.
agent_relevance: A store of no-goods can encode shortcuts that tree search cannot. The gain needs a good choice of what to try first.

source: Atserias, Fichte, Thurley (2011) Clause-learning algorithms with many restarts and bounded-width resolution
finding: A solver with unit propagation, clause learning and restarts behaves like width-k resolution with high probability after a bounded number of conflicts and restarts.
numbers: Bound: no more than O(n^(2k+2)) conflicts and restarts, n = number of variables.
limits: Proof for an idealised solver with random choices; not an empirical test.
agent_relevance: Explains why restarts pair with learning: a restart gives a new start while the stored lessons persist. A restart that keeps the lessons is not a reset.

source: Liang, Ganesh, Zulkoski, Zaman, Czarnecki (2015) Understanding VSIDS branching heuristics in CDCL SAT solvers
finding: VSIDS tends to pick bridge variables between instance communities, and it works partly because it favours variables that recently produced good learned clauses (an exponential moving average). The authors built a variant that adapts to learned clause quality.
numbers: adaptVSIDS solved 2.4% more instances than mVSIDS on the SAT Competition 2013 benchmarks.
limits: Gain is small. Mechanism shown by correlation on solver runs.
agent_relevance: Choose what to try next by where conflicts recently happened, not at random.

source: Elffers, Giraldez-Cru, Gocht, Nordstrom, Simon (2018) Seeking practical CDCL insights from theoretical SAT benchmarks
finding: Crafted benchmarks from proof-complexity theory are used to test which solver parts matter in practice. Only the title page was read this session.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not opened beyond the first page.
agent_relevance: Possible source on whether short proofs are found in practice; read before use.

source: Zhang, Chen, Chen (2026) Satisfiability solving with LLMs: a matched-pair evaluation of reasoning capability (FSE 2026)
finding: Most LLMs say 'satisfiable' for nearly every random 3-SAT formula and do not show the easy-hard-easy phase transition that CDCL shows. A paired test (a SAT and an UNSAT formula that differ minimally) exposes this: accuracy looks high, paired success is low.
numbers: 2700+ 3-SAT formulas; models include GPT-5, o1, o3-mini, DeepSeek-reasoner, Claude 3 to 4 variants, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5. Non-reasoning models fall below paired score (ADR) 0.2 by 25 variables. GPT-5 ADR 0.79 at 25 variables, 0.35 at 50 (only about 20% of runs completed). Always predicting SAT gives accuracy 0.5 but ADR 0.
quote: models tend to classify all formulas as satisfiable
limits: Random SAT and 2-SAT, plus vertex cover and 3D packing reductions. Few repetitions. GPT-5 timeouts at larger sizes.
agent_relevance: A language model alone is a poor search engine and a poor UNSAT prover. Proofs that a region is exhausted must come from code, not from the model's claim. Supports G2 and G3.

source: Zhang, Chen, Chen (2026) matched-pair SAT evaluation: self-reported search effort and representation
finding: Model-reported 'branches' and 'conflicts' did not track CDCL hardness. Decisions on CNF and on its vertex-cover or packing form agreed on over 80% of instances for most models, but GPT-5 scored far lower on vertex cover.
numbers: At 25 variables GPT-5 paired score 0.79 on SAT versus about 0.27 on vertex cover. GPT-5 with a 3D-packing reduction at 30 variables: F1 0.77 but paired score 0.60.
limits: Self-report columns were excluded from main results by the authors.
agent_relevance: Never use the model's own count of how much it searched as a budget or stop signal. Count in code.

source: Pan, Ganesh, Abernethy, Esposo, Lee (2025) Can transformers reason logically? A study in SAT solving (ICML 2025)
finding: Decoder-only transformers can in theory decide 3-SAT with chain-of-thought using DPLL-style backtracking and deduction. Small models (70M and 160M LLaMA-style) trained on DPLL traces reach near-perfect accuracy within the trained size range but fail on more variables than seen in training. The traces are DPLL, not CDCL.
numbers: Trained on 6-10 or 11-15 variables, 5x10^5 samples each. Within range: 98.5% to 99.96% SAT/UNSAT accuracy on most test distributions; lowest about 86% to 93% on the hardest set. Beyond range accuracy drops sharply (tested 4 to 20 variables, 2000 samples each).
limits: From-scratch tiny models on one algorithm. Says nothing about prompting a frontier model. No learned-clause traces.
agent_relevance: A model can follow an explicit backtracking procedure if it is trained on it, but it does not extend it to longer problems. The program should own the loop and the lessons.

source: Sun, Ye, Zhang, Huang, Zhang, Wei, Cai (2024) AutoSAT: automatically optimize SAT solvers via LLMs (JAIR)
finding: An LLM rewrites the heuristic functions of a CDCL solver (EasySAT), guided by greedy hill climbing or a (1+1) evolutionary loop, and each candidate is scored by PAR-2 on a dataset. Real gains on some families, none on others.
numbers: Beats MiniSat on 9 of 12 datasets and Kissat on 4 (paper's wording). PAR-2 with solved count: cryptography-ascon 503 (20) baseline vs 215 (20); PRP 10,000 (0) vs 5,204 (10); MineSweeper 3,886 (63) vs 1,608 (83).
limits: Gains are over the base solver and tuned variants on chosen families. Hill climbing stalls in local optima. Success rests on the score from running code.
agent_relevance: An LLM improves a CDCL component only because a code-run score picks the result (G5, G8). The model proposes, the run decides.

source: Sun, Ye, Chen, Wei, Cai (2026, v2) Discovering heuristics in a complex SAT solver with LLMs (AutoModSAT)
finding: A modular solver layout, prompt diversification and a (1+lambda) search let an LLM improve a large CDCL solver, with gains over the base and over parameter-tuned state-of-the-art solvers.
numbers: About 40% PAR-2 improvement over base ModSAT; 30% speedup over parameter-tuned ModSAT; more than 30% average gain against Kissat and CaDiCaL; matches or beats tuned versions on solved counts in 8 of 11 datasets (authors' claims).
limits: Authors' own benchmark choice; three seeds per run shown.
agent_relevance: An LLM can edit solver heuristics when code keeps a hard score. It is not an LLM that runs CDCL in text.

source: Chen and Li (2025) DaSAThco: data-aware SAT heuristics combinations via LLMs
finding: An LLM generates a portfolio of CDCL heuristic ensembles (restart, phase, bump) per problem archetype and a learned selector picks one per instance. A single tuned solver can still win in-domain.
numbers: 1000 s timeout, PAR-2. The paper reports more instances solved than AutoSAT on CoinsGrid (AutoSAT solved 15). In-domain, the single best tuned solver can still be best.
limits: I did not extract every table cell. Few datasets.
agent_relevance: Echoes our portfolio rule: no single method wins everywhere; select per problem signal.

source: Sarkar (2026) From errors to proofs: minimal-core-guided repair for neuro-symbolic constraint solving
finding: The LLM writes an ASP encoding. On UNSAT the loop returns a minimal unsatisfiable core of the model's own constraints instead of a bare error. This is the nearest published LLM-loop analogue of conflict analysis. The accuracy gain is small; the main gain is that a weaker model stops deleting real constraints to escape UNSAT.
numbers: 77 problems with exact oracle, repair budget K=3. Repair lifts the pipeline from 84.4% to 89.6% (gemma4:31b); generic-error repair 88.3% vs core repair 89.6% (sign test p=1.0, no difference). deepseek-v3.2 fabricates a solution on 11 of 14 infeasible problems (79%) with generic feedback vs 1 of 14 (7%) with a core (Fisher p<0.001). Direct prompting 74.0% feasibility, fabricates on 3 of 14 (21.4%); chain-of-thought 98.7%.
limits: One independent author, templated problems, only 14 infeasible instances. Chain-of-thought is hard to beat on accuracy at these sizes.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2: give the model the exact minimal set that cannot hold together, computed by code. Without it a weaker model destroys constraints to escape the conflict.

source: Salla, Amancherla, Saravanan (2026) Quantifying cross-query contradictions in multi-query LLM reasoning (ICLR 2026 workshop)
finding: An LLM's answers across related queries are checked for joint satisfiability with SAT/SMT. On UNSAT an unsat core points to the clashing commitments and only those are repaired. Core-guided repair beats retrying without a core.
numbers: 390 instances, four domains. Set consistency 0.56 to 0.94 overall. Ablation (deep subset): no solver acc 0.77, SetCons 0.52; check-only 0.78 / 0.84; repair without core 0.79 / 0.88 / revision cost 0.6; core-guided 0.81 / 0.91 / revision cost 0.4. Overhead 1.51x.
limits: Workshop paper, authors' own benchmark, solver validation on 50 cases (13%).
agent_relevance: Keep a set of commitments, test it for consistency in code, and revise only the clashing subset. Same shape as a no-good.

source: Shinn, Cassano, Berman, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: After a failed trial the agent writes a short verbal reflection and carries it in memory (usually 1 to 3 stored experiences) into the next trial. This is a soft, natural-language version of a stored no-good.
numbers: ALFWorld: ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks, +22% absolute over baseline within 12 trials; ReAct alone plateaus with a 22% hallucination rate. HotPotQA +20%. HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%.
limits: Failure verdicts come from the environment or unit tests. Memory capped at 1-3 reflections. Reflections are free text, not checked rules.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of 'learn a clause from a conflict and keep it across restarts'. It works when the failure signal is real; see Huang et al.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: self-evaluation trigger
finding: For ALFWorld the failure trigger was a code heuristic: the same action with the same response more than 3 times, or more than 30 actions. Baseline runs reset and retry without a reflection.
numbers: Thresholds: 3 repeated cycles, 30 actions.
limits: Hand-written for one environment.
agent_relevance: A cheap code-side impasse detector that decides when to store a lesson (G1).

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Self-correction gains reported earlier depended on oracle labels that tell the model when it is wrong. Without them, self-correction lowers accuracy.
numbers: Standard vs oracle self-correction (GSM8K / CommonSenseQA / HotpotQA): GPT-3.5 75.9 / 75.8 / 26.0 to 84.3 / 89.7 / 29.0; GPT-4 95.5 / 82.0 / 49.0 to 97.5 / 85.5 / 59.0. No oracle, GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 then 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0 over rounds. 74.7% of GPT-3.5 GSM8K answers unchanged.
limits: Few benchmarks, prompts from earlier work. Table row labels were garbled in text extraction; the row-to-model mapping is inferred from Table 3. Later work found gains with external verifiers.
agent_relevance: A lesson is only as good as the failure signal behind it. Store a no-good only after a code check says the attempt failed (G2).

source: Bonagiri et al. (2026) CausalFlow: causal attribution and counterfactual repair for LLM agent failures
finding: A failed trace is cut down to the failure-inducing step by replacing each step in turn and re-running. The minimal edit that flips the result to success is kept as a validated pair. This mirrors conflict analysis that finds the responsible decisions.
numbers: 3004 problems, four benchmarks; 1299 failed; 555 repaired (42.7%); repair rate 21.9% (SealQA Hard) to 52.4% (GSM8K). MedBrowseComp accuracy 30.8% to 61.6%; SealQA Hard 42.5% to 55.1%. Exception MBPP: Self-Refine repaired 80.3%, Self-Reflection 56.4%, CausalFlow 41.2%. GSM8K typed-trace format cost accuracy: 75.0% initial vs 88.1% direct. Gains level off after K=3 interventions.
limits: Preprint; repairs checked by the benchmark checker; typed logging costs accuracy on easy tasks.
agent_relevance: Credit assignment by re-running the trace is the agent version of 1-UIP analysis. It costs extra runs and logging.

source: Ji, Lu, Zhang, Olukotun (2026) Sentry: learning to recover from LLM agent failures at test time
finding: Failure lessons are conditional rules. Kept in context all the time they misfire and lower performance. Sentry detects a failure, retrieves only the matching lesson from an external store, checks without task rewards that the agent recovered, and stores a new lesson only if it did.
numbers: Beats the strongest runtime-intervention baseline by 37% on average (up to 77% on WebShop) and ACE by 39% on two benchmarks. Removing failure lessons from ACE's playbook raised reward 0.335 to 0.391 (WebShop) and 0.562 to 0.643 (Mind2Web Replay). A fixed playbook in persistent context: WebShop reward 0.364 to 0.296. Resolves 81.7% of 939 detected failures; action-validity failures 92.6%; SWE-bench Lite progress 34.0%.
limits: Preprint, one group. Recovery check is an LLM judge over the next 10 cycles. Web and tool tasks.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for our design: keep the lesson store outside the prompt and show a lesson only when a matching failure signal fires (G1). Full no-good lists in context hurt.

source: Ji et al. (2026) Sentry: ablations
finding: Each part of the pipeline matters. Removing soft repair, the intervention-need check, failure-specific retrieval or recovery verification all cost performance. Random lesson retrieval is worse than no filter.
numbers: Local recovery 33.5% to 60.5% with Sentry; intervened branch scored higher in 74 of the matched pairs. Removing the intervention-need check costs 54.7% on average over two benchmarks; w/o soft repair WebShop reward 0.136 (-70.9%). Dropping failure-type filter -11.3%, unfiltered playbook -18.8%, random entries -28.9%; k=10 or more lessons costs 4.5% to 6.2% vs k=5. Human agreement 86.0% (200 windows) and 81.8% (99 judgments).
limits: Same group and judge model family; ablation sizes small.
agent_relevance: Retrieve few (about 5) matching lessons, verify recovery by code before saving. Mirrors clause deletion: keep only useful learned clauses.

source: Yan et al. (2026) TIDE: trajectory-based diagnostic evaluation of test-time improvement in LLM agents
finding: Many agents repeat the same failed action instead of adapting. Loop Ratio (share of redundant loop actions) is high in small models and tracks poor improvement over time. Larger models loop less.
numbers: Qwen3-4B-Instruct loop ratio 32.0% in FrozenLake. Qwen3-4B to Qwen3-30B-A3B cuts loop ratio from 15.8% to 1.0% in BlocksWorld and 36.7% to 5.7% in WebShop. DeepSeek and Gemini series negligible. High loop ratio goes with low Area Under Variation (significant inverse relation across four models).
limits: Five environments; loop detected by a finite-state rule; correlational.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the problem a no-good list addresses (repeating a refuted attempt). A code-side repeat detector is cheap and can trigger the impasse path.

source: An et al. (2024) Learn from failure: fine-tuning LLMs with trial-and-error data for intuitionistic propositional logic proving (TrialMaster)
finding: A prover trained on whole search trees, including failed branches and explicit backtrack instructions, uses fewer proof-assistant calls than a standard DFS around a tactic generator trained on successful paths only. Failed attempts are visible in the prompt so refuted tactics are avoided.
numbers: In-distribution (Llama-7b, Lean): TrialMaster 100% success; DFS 99.5% to 99.9% at best settings, 75.9% at 2 sampled tactics, 97.3% at 5, 99.0% at 10. Out of distribution TrialMaster beats DFS at every tried setting (values only in a figure I did not extract). Step limit 65; context limit 1500 words.
limits: Small domain, fine-tuning needed, 1500-word cap limits the format.
agent_relevance: A short log of refuted moves in context cuts search cost for provers, but here it is trained in. A prompt-only copy is untested.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Where LLM agents fail and how they can learn from failures (AgentDebug)
finding: Root-cause failure isolation plus corrective feedback lets agents recover. Seen as a search snippet only; the PDF download was truncated.
numbers: Snippet: up to 26% relative gain in task success on ALFWorld, GAIA and WebShop.
limits: Not opened. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Second source for root-cause isolation before storing a lesson.

source: SciAgentGym, LLM-WikiRace, Robotouille (2025-2026) loop and recovery metrics (search snippets)
finding: Other agent benchmarks measure stuck or repeated behaviour. Seen only in search snippets; PDFs were truncated.
numbers: Snippets: SciAgentGym loop escape 35.7%; LLM-WikiRace recovery near 0 on the hardest split, best 12%; Robotouille 90% (9) of recovered failures not repeated on the synchronous set and 57.1% (12) on the asynchronous set.
limits: Not opened. Verify before use.
agent_relevance: Context for how common repeated failure is in agent loops.

source: Drescher and Walsh; Dechter and others: nogood learning in CSP, ASP and planning (search result titles)
finding: CSP, ASP (lazy nogood generation) and planning have close relatives of CDCL. Only titles and snippets were seen.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Open gap: no source found that tests nogood-style generalised lessons in an LLM loop.
agent_relevance: Likely source for how to generalise a lesson from one failed attempt to a class of attempts.
